b.bio: Francesco Petrarca, born at Arezzo on 20 July 1304 and died at Arquà on 19 July 1374, was an Italian scholar and poet trained at Montpellier (1319–23) and Bologna (1323–25) for law, though he abandoned law for letters. He spent much of his career in Avignon and its region during the papal residence there, and his recovery of Cicero's letters is credited with launching Renaissance humanism. The work held here is his prolegomenon to Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos: it surveys citations from classical authors — Varro, Terence, Livy, Ovid — and argues that Augustine's psalms commentary stands unmatched in magnitude among Latin works, the fruit of a conversion that yielded divine knowledge and tireless writing.
b.s: His preface frames Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos as the largest achievement of Latin Christian letters, written by the humanist who set the terms for reading the ancients alongside the Fathers.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Francesco Ambrogi; they concern a modern fluid-dynamics professor at Queen's University, the humanist Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi, Francis of Fabriano, and the antiquary Francesco Angeloni — different people entirely, to be ignored here. The library record itself is the only evidence: a sixteen-page Latin apologetic preface printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 178, defending Peter Abelard against Bernard of Clairvaux.
b.s: His preface is an apology for Abelard, arguing that Abelard was falsely accused of heresy and deserves defense, that the chapters condemned at Sens were disowned unheard, that the burning of his book was an obedient act rather than a condemnation, that Innocent granted him full absolution — while also preferring Baronius over Gregory of Tours on the Dionysii.

b.t: Gothic philology (edited under Latin Fathers shelf)
b.bio: Tempestinus, F. (unknown) — No surviving record identifies a person named Tempestinus, F. The Du Cange entry under 'Tempestarii' concerns weather-working sorcerers in capitularies and penitentials, not an author; the other sources describe Victorinus of Pettau, Faustinus the Luciferian presbyter, and Fulgentius — none of whom match works like those held here. The library record is therefore the only guide: under this name it holds two philological treatises on the Gothic language, citing Grimm, Bopp, Massmann, Ihre, and Aschbach, and arguing against Castiglioni, Manso, Zeuss, and Reiske. This apparatus places the composition in the nineteenth century, but no source gives dates, birthplace, or office for the author.
b.s: The works here are a Gothic grammar and glossary asserting that Gothic is the oldest written Germanic language, that its primitive vowel is 'a', that the Goths are of Germanic origin with a common speech, and that Ptolemy's and Procopius's ethnonyms denote Scandinavian Goths.

b.bio: Francisco Pérez Bayer was born in Valencia in 1711 and died there in 1794. A priest and philologist who studied Philosophy and Theology at the University of Valencia and Arts and Civil Law at Salamanca, he held the Chair of Hebrew at Valencia from 1745 and took the same chair at Salamanca in 1746. He served as secretary to the Archbishop of Valencia; after a royal commission to review the Archivos of Toledo (1750), Fernando VI awarded him a canonry in Barcelona and sent him to Italy to collect manuscripts, coins, and inscriptions. Carlos III later commissioned him to inventory the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew manuscripts of El Escorial. He was a critic and editor of ancient texts rather than a systematic theologian.
b.s: The work held here is his Roman dissertation of 1756 arguing, against Blanchini, Merenda, and others, that Pope Damasus I and the martyr Lawrence were Spaniards by birth — a thesis grounded in ancient testimony and codices over modern conjecture.

w: Apology for the Chronicle of Dexter

b.bio: Francisco de Bivar was born at Paracuellos de Jarama in 1584 and took the Cistercian habit at Santa María de Nogales (León), studying philosophy at San Clodio and theology at Salamanca. He served as chaplain to the convent of Santa Ana at Valladolid, was his Order's procurator in Rome from 1620 — where he worked three years in the Vatican Library on the origins of monasticism and the Hispanic sanctoral — and died as abbot of Sacramenia at the Cistercian house in Madrid. Sources give differing death dates: 1634 (Spanish Wikipedia, Bibale), 1635 (Online Books Page), or 1636 (McClintock & Strong); McClintock & Strong also gives his birthplace as Madrid rather than Paracuellos. His chief claim on attention is unfortunate: he edited and defended the forged chronicles of Flavius Lucius Dexter concocted by Jerónimo Román de la Higuera.
b.s: The works held here are Bivar's apologies for the pseudo-Dexter Chronicle — a Higuera forgery he defended against Pennottus and other detractors, arguing that Jerome's attestation of Dexter, public reception by Spanish prelates, and a supposed Fulda codex transmitted from Toledo (via Elipandus, with Julian of Peter confirming the transfer) established its authority.

b.bio: The library holds one three-page addition to the Bec Chronicle under this name, printed in PL 150. The supplied biographical sources describe other men entirely: a twentieth-century Dominican preacher and Académie française member named Ambroise-Marie Carré, and a seventeenth-century Jesuit historian named François Catrou; neither can be the author of a medieval monastic chronicle from Bec, so they are set aside. Nothing in the record or any source establishes this author's dates, office, or life.
b.s: The fragment is a short monastic history recording the Virgin's intervention against plague at Bec, the expulsion of John Ribaldus for moral laxity, canon-law arguments against alienating church property, and the claim that exile for the church is sweet to endure.

b.bio: Fernando del Castillo was born in Granada around 1529 and entered the Dominican Order at the convent of San Pablo in Valladolid on September 17, 1544, professing before Fray Juan Manuel. He studied arts and theology at Valladolid and at the Colegio de San Gregorio, taught cases of conscience at Logroño, and rose to be a preacher at court, preceptor of the infant Ferdinand, professor of theology in houses of his order, a member of the Tribunal of the Inquisition, and a counselor of Philip II. He died in Madrid on March 29, 1593. His principal work was the Historia General de Santo Domingo (1584–1592). The library holds under his name only an eight-page Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The work held here is a short hagiographical life of Peter Chrysologus that supplies the biographical frame for reading Chrysologus's sermons: it asserts his birth at Forum Cornelii (Imola) in Aemilia, his naming for his 'golden eloquence,' and his preaching against Eutyches and Nestorius; notably, it argues against the tradition that Chrysologus initially refused the see of Ravenna.

b.t: French jurist and historian of Franche-Comté
b.bio: François-Ignace Dunod de Charnage was born at Saint-Claude on 30 October 1679 and died at Besançon on 21 June 1752. An avocat at the Parlement of Besançon, he taught law at the University of Besançon from December 1720 and served as its rector. He wrote works on jurisprudence — prescriptions, alienation of church property, tithes, mortmain — and historical works on Burgundy and Franche-Comté, including an Histoire du Comté de Bourgogne (Dijon, 1735). He is not a patristic author; the shelf label 'Latin Fathers' does not describe him.
b.s: The single page this library holds under his name is a historical notice, not one of his legal or historical treatises; readers should know him as an eighteenth-century Burgundian jurist rather than a church father.

b.bio: Falco of Benevento was a Lombard notary and scribe in the papal palace of his native Benevento. His chronicle covers the years 1102 to 1139 in southern Italy, much of it from eyewitness observation. He was a partisan writer: proud of Benevento, hostile to the Normans as barbarians, an opponent of King Roger II of Sicily, and a supporter of Pope Innocent II against the antipope Anacletus II. His loyalty to Innocent cost him exile from Benevento in 1134. Parts of his chronicle are lost, though they were apparently used for 1099–1103 and 1140–49 by the Chronica Romanorum pontificum et imperatorum.
b.s: The Chronicle held here is a primary narrative for Norman expansion in the Mezzogiorno and the schism of 1130, arguing from a Lombard, pro-Innocent II standpoint against Roger II and Anacletus.

b.bio: A Lombard who came to the Frankish kingdom after Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard realm in 774, Fardulf served the king and was rewarded with the abbacy of Saint-Denis near Paris in 792. He held it until his death in 806. The verses preserved under his name include inscriptions for buildings at Saint-Denis and a church of John the Baptist, composed after his restoration to favor under Charles.
b.s: The library holds his Carmina (PL 99), short poems on Saint-Denis and its patron that commemorate royal benefaction and speak of the saints' merits, commemoration of the dead, and eternal life.

b.bio: Faro (Burgundofaro) came from a noble Burgundian family; his father Agneric was a chief counselor to Theodebert II, his brother Chagnoald was bishop of Laon, and his sister Burgundofara founded Faremoutiers. Raised at court, he served Theodebert II, Theodoric, and Clotaire II before entering the clergy. He became bishop of Meaux in 627 and held the see until his death around 675. He is honored as a saint in the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
b.s: The library holds only two pages under his name: charters printed in PL 87, which touch on the Church, true worship, and the sacraments as historical documents rather than theological treatises.

w: Letter on the Council of Toulouse

b.bio: Fastred of Clairvaux was born at Cambron (in the diocese of Cambrai, Belgium) and entered the abbey of Clairvaux as a monk under Bernard of Clairvaux. He founded the monastery at Cambron in 1148, became abbot of Clairvaux in 1157, and in 1161 the seventh abbot of Cîteaux. A supporter of Pope Alexander III against Frederick Barbarossa, he died in Paris on April 21, 1163, having traveled there to meet Pope Alexander and advocate Bernard's canonization.
b.s: The two letters held here are among the few surviving writings of a Cistercian abbot who led both Clairvaux and Cîteaux in the generation after Bernard.

b.bio: Faustus was born in Britain between about 400 and 410, according to his contemporaries Avitus of Vienne and Sidonius Apollinaris. He entered the monastery of Lérins in southern Gaul, became its head around 432–433 in succession to Maximus, and succeeded Maximus as bishop of Riez around 458. He opposed Arianism and played a leading role in the ecclesiastical life of fifth-century Gaul. The works held here defend a middle position on grace: against Pelagius he insists salvation depends on God's drawing mercy, yet against the predestinarians he argues that the will can precede special grace and that grace alone and human labor alone are twin errors.
b.s: He is one of the chief surviving exponents and defenders of the semi-Pelagian position on grace and free will in fifth-century Gaul, and the treatise here is a classic statement of it.

b.bio: Faustus of Mileve was a Manichaean bishop from Milevis in Numidia (modern Algeria), of poor pagan background, who became the sect's most reputed teacher and debater in the region. Augustine of Hippo met him at Carthage around 383 and found him eloquent but unable to answer his questions about Manichaean doctrine — an encounter Augustine records in the Confessions and credits with hastening his break with Manichaeism. About 400 Faustus published an attack on the Catholic faith, known as the Capitula, which survives only because Augustine quoted it entire in his Contra Faustum Manichaeum.
b.s: His anti-Catholic capitula survive solely through Augustine's book-by-book citation and refutation, making him the best-attested voice of Latin Manichaeism and a principal foil of Augustine's polemic.

w: Fragment of a confession of faith

b.bio: Felix I succeeded Dionysius as bishop of Rome early in 269 and held that office until his death on 30 December 274. His papacy coincided with the Synod of Antioch's deposition of Paul of Samosata in 269; a dogmatic letter on the Trinity and the unity of Christ's person circulated under Felix's name in response. The Catholic Encyclopedia identifies the letter preserved in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus as spurious, later interpolated by a follower of Apollinaris in the interest of that sect. The martyrdom attributed to him in the Liber Pontificalis is unsupported by ancient authority; he was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus.
b.s: The fragment held here — a confession asserting that Christ is the eternal Word incarnate, one person who is perfect God and perfect man, against Adoptionists — is, on the Catholic Encyclopedia's account, an interpolated text transmitted under Felix's name and read at Ephesus in 431.

b.bio: Felix of Samnium, son of Castorius, was consecrated bishop of Rome on 12 July 526 as the choice of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, whose predecessor John I had died in prison at Ravenna. After Theodoric's death on 30 August 526, Felix governed under Amalasuntha's regency; an edict drawn up by Cassiodorus confirmed that charges brought by laymen against clergy were to be judged by the pope or an ecclesiastical court appointed by him. He built the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano in the Roman forums and defined teaching on grace and free will against Semi-Pelagianism. The works printed under his name in PL 65 include material whose attribution to Felix II or Felix III is disputed.
b.s: The library holds his letters and decrees on clerical discipline — probation of ordinands, good testimony from outsiders, episcopal revenues for household and hospitality — plus an appendix addressing the attribution disputes among popes named Felix.

b.bio: The library holds one epistle under this name in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 87), but no surviving record identifies its author. The name must not be confused with Marcus Minucius Felix, the early Latin apologist of Berber origin who lived in Rome as a lawyer, wrote the Octavius, and died in or about 250 (source 1); that man is a different figure entirely. Nor does he match Martial, first bishop of Limoges (source 4), or Sacerdos, a later bishop of Limoges (source 3), described in the other sources.
b.s: The single work held here is an epistle printed in PL 87; beyond its presence in that volume, the sources give no account of its author or contents.

w: Prologue to the Sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus

b.bio: Felix was archbishop of Ravenna from 709 until his death. Sources disagree on the year of death: Wikipedia gives 724, while the Deutsche Biographie index gives 716. He was consecrated by Pope Constantine but soon asserted independence from Rome; after Justinian II captured Ravenna he was taken to Constantinople, tried, blinded, and exiled to Pontus, returning after Justinian's deposition in 711. He collected 176 sermons of his predecessor Peter Chrysologus.
b.s: The work held here is his prologue to the sermons of Peter Chrysologus, which commends Chrysologus as a doctor of Catholic truth and urges reading the fathers for eternal reward.

b.bio: Felix first appears securely as a signatory to the Thirteenth Council of Toledo (683) as abbot or archpriest (the codices vary on his dignity), and again at the Fourteenth (684) and Fifteenth (688) Councils as archpriest. He was named bishop of Seville around 688 and elevated to the see of Toledo in 693 by King Egica after the deposition and imprisonment of Sisberto, confirmed there by the Sixteenth Council of Toledo (2 May 693). He held Toledo until his death, probably in 702; the Chronica Muzarabica of 754 records him celebrating councils during the joint reign of Egica and Witiza, probably the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Councils of Toledo (694 and 702). He is not the same person as Felix of Urgel (died 818), the Adoptionist bishop condemned at Regensburg and Frankfurt and opposed by Alcuin.
b.s: The works held here are hagiographical and doctrinal pieces from late Visigothic Spain: a Life of St. Julian arguing that saintly friends possess one soul in charity and that divine providence redirects contemplatives to active service, and a Confession of Faith treating the church (marked by episcopal succession), resurrection, last things, and Christ's birth shown from scripture without chronological computation.

b.bio: Felix was bishop of Urgell in the Pyrenees and, with Archbishop Elipandus of Toledo, the chief proponent of Spanish Adoptionism — the teaching that Christ, as man, was the adopted rather than natural Son of God. Condemned by Pope Adrian I, he was summoned by Charlemagne to the Council of Regensburg in 792 and induced to recant; the condemnation was renewed at Frankfurt in 794. He returned to Urgell and engaged in a doctrinal duel with Alcuin of York before dying in 818. His adoptionist writings were suppressed and survive only in quotations from opponents.
b.s: The Confession of Faith held here is Felix's own recantation: he renounces his former adoptionist teaching, affirming that Christ is Son by nature not adoption, that the Word assumed a complete human nature with a rational soul without conversion of either nature into the other, and that patristic authority and the consent of the church convict error.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Flavius Constantinus', but the held work does not match the famous fourth-century emperor Constantine I (Flavius Valerius Constantinus). The epistle in PL 87 cites Pope Agatho, Domnus, the five holy synods, opposes Theodorus of Constantinople and Macarius of theopolis, and asserts that the emperor is guardian of the received faith. These features point to a seventh-century Byzantine emperor writing in connection with the Monothelite controversy, not to Constantine the Great. No surviving record gives dates for this author, so none are asserted.
b.s: The single held epistle is an imperial letter on the Monothelite dispute, arguing that the five synods and approved fathers completed the faith, that faith must be persuaded rather than compelled, and that providence overrules human deliberation.

b.bio: Gundemar was a Visigothic king of Hispania, Septimania and Galicia who reigned from about April 610 to February or March 612, succeeding Witteric and followed by Sisebut. He was a Chalcedonian Christian; his wife was Hildoara. The library holds a single page under his name: a decree asserting the primacy of the Toledan see over the province of Carthaginiensis against bishops contesting it, including one Euphemius. The document argues that one metropolitan per province preserves unity, that Carpetania belongs to the Carthaginian province, that royal power enforces ecclesiastical discipline, and that the kingdom is governed by divine guidance through piety.
b.s: His decree is an early royal intervention fixing Toledo's metropolitan primacy, a step toward the see's later dominance in the Visigothic church.

b.bio:
Flavius Josephus (c. 37–c. 100) — Yosef ben Mattityahu, a Jerusalem priest of aristocratic descent, commanded Jewish forces in Galilee in the revolt of 66–67, surrendered to Vespasian at Yodfat, and after Vespasian became emperor took the name Flavius and wrote under Roman patronage. His Greek works—the Jewish War and the Antiquities of the Jews—circulated widely in Latin translation through the Middle Ages. The four-page Book of Hebrew Names printed here under his name is a Latin onomastic treatise explaining the meanings of Hebrew proper names; it cites Jerome and argues that transmitted name-forms are often corrupt against the Hebrew, so the sense of sacred names must be recovered by Hebrew etymology.

Jerome of Stridon (c. c. 340–420) — Jerome (Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus) was born at Stridon, a town on the confines of Dalmatia and Pannonia; sources give his birth between about 340-2 and 347. He was educated at Rome and baptized there (probably around 360, or about 366 per Benedict XVI), lived as an ascetic in the desert of Chalcis (374-379), was ordained priest at Antioch, spent 382-385 in Rome in close association with Pope Damasus, then settled at Bethlehem in 386, where he died on 30 September 420. He learned Hebrew and produced a Latin Bible translated from the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint (the Vulgate), commentaries, polemical essays, and historical work.
b.s: The work held here is not his history but an etymological dictionary of biblical names transmitted under his authority, used by medieval readers to interpret Scripture through Hebrew word-meanings.

b.bio: The name Florentius covers several distinct figures: a 5th-century bishop of Sardis who attended the Council of Chalcedon (fl. 451) and served on its drafting subcommittee; an Anomoean rival archbishop of Constantinople under Jovian (c. 363); and Georgius Florentius, Gregory of Tours (c. 538–594). None of these source accounts describes a letter to Lucifer arguing that books offered to the emperor must be orthodox, so the author of the single page held here cannot be identified with confidence from the material given.
b.s: The library holds one page of a letter to Lucifer asserting that books offered to the emperor must be orthodox; its attribution within the name Florentius remains unresolved against surviving records.

b.bio: The library's single work under this name is a sixth-century epistle addressed by Florianus, a monk of the monastery of Romanum (al. Remano), to Nicetius, whom he addresses as pope ('Domino suo Nicetio papae'). The letter praises Nicetius for his cenobitic training from boyhood, his victory over the 'Amalech' of the spiritual life, his humility after the pattern of Elijah and the apostles on the mount of Transfiguration, and asks him to intercede in prayer. The text cites Ennodius of Pavia (Ticinum), Caesarius of Arles, Ambrose, and Paul. This is not Florus the deacon of Lyons (ninth century) nor Florinus the second-century Roman presbyter deprived for heresy; those homonyms belong elsewhere.
b.s: The held work is a one-page epistle on prayer and intercession that asserts Mary is both Christotokos and Theotokos and argues against Nestorius and Eutyches.

b.bio: The library's author is Folcardus Lobiensis, abbot of the imperial abbey of Lobbes, attested in office from 1094 to 1107. He is not the same man as Folcard the Flemish hagiographer, monk of St Bertin and putative abbot of Thorney, who died after 1085; that earlier Folcard wrote saints' lives in England and Flanders and must not be confused with him. The abbot of Lobbes appears in the Patrologia Latina with a single epistle addressed to Emperor Henry.
b.s: His Epistle XIV to Emperor Henry is a polemical letter defending Saint Peter's abbey against its advocates — including the castellan, the countess of Mons, and Henry of Marbais — arguing that royal grants secure the monks' ancient liberty, that the advocate's fee is fixed at the third denarius by joint appraisal, and that mercy and judgment please God more than sacrifice while justice departs the land.

w: Life of St. John of Beverley
Sermon on the feast of St. Bertin

b.bio: Folcard, a Fleming, was a monk of Saint-Bertin in Flanders who came to England in the reign of Edward the Confessor and entered Christ Church, Canterbury, where he was known for grammar and music. After the Conquest the king set him over Thorney Abbey, though he never received abbatial benediction; after some sixteen years he retired following a dispute with Remigius, Bishop of Lincoln, and apparently returned to Flanders. He wrote the Life of St. John of Beverley for Archbishop Aldred of York in return for Aldred's help when his monastery was in trouble. Some scholars also credit him with the Vita Ædwardi Regis on Edward the Confessor, though others assign it to Goscelin.
b.s: The works held here are his hagiography: lives and miracles of St. Bertin, a life of St. John of Beverley, a poem on St. Vigor, and a sermon for Bertin's feast, written to commend worthy predecessors and defend the cult against critics such as Fridogisus.

w: Life of Saint Folcuin of Thérouanne
On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes

b.bio: Folcuin (c. 935 – 16 September 990) became a monk at Saint-Bertin near Thérouanne in 948, where he was a deacon and archivist, and was designated abbot of Lobbes in 965 by Bishop Everaclus of Liège. He wrote histories of the abbots of both monasteries. That the monk of Saint-Bertin and the abbot of Lobbes were one man was only rediscovered in 1881. His intelligent use of documentary evidence and his distrust of mere oral tradition give him special importance as a writer.
b.s: The works here are his cartulary-history of Saint-Bertin's abbots (Gesta abbatum Sithiensium), his Gesta abbatum Lobiensium, and a life of his great-uncle, Bishop Folcuin of Thérouanne — histories that weave charters into narrative under a providential reading of events.

b.bio: Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus was born between 530 and 540 near Treviso in northern Italy and educated at Ravenna. He left Ravenna around 565 and traveled through the Rhineland—Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Metz—reaching Poitiers in 567, where he attached himself to the circle of Radegunda and her monastery of the Holy Cross. He became bishop of Poitiers and died there c. 600 or 609. Sources give slightly different birth and death dates (Britannica: c. 540–c. 600; Wikipedia: c. 530–c. 600/609). His Latin poems and hymns combine classical models with a medieval tone.
b.s: A transitional poet between antiquity and the Middle Ages, he is best known for hymns still in use. The single page of his occasional verse held here (PL 80) is catalogued as 'Verses to Bertichramnus'; its specific contents are not described in surviving records.

w: Hymn for St. Nicholas the Pilgrim

b.bio: No source identifies a writer named Franciscus Camenus. The surviving records describe four unrelated men — Franciscus Quaresmius, Johannes Campensis, Franciscus Lucas Brugensis, and Franciscus van den Enden — none of whom matches this name or the work held here, so they are set aside. What the library record shows is a single-page Latin hymn for St. Nicholas the Pilgrim (d. Trani, 1094), printed in PL 162, narrating the saint's miracles of healing and deliverance and affirming the Trinity and the visible assistance of angels to holy men.
b.s: The library holds only this one-page hymn from PL 162, a devotional account of the miracles of St. Nicholas the Pilgrim rather than a doctrinal treatise.

w: On the Squaring of the Circle

b.bio: Franco of Liège was an eleventh-century mathematician and cathedral official at Saint Lambert's in Liège: chancellor by 1057, scholaster from before 1066 until his death around 1083. His De quadratura circuli, written about 1050, recounts his attempt to square the circle, including cutting a parchment circle into pieces to reassemble as a square. Sigebert of Gembloux also credits him with saints' lives, a poem on the wood of the cross, and a treatise on the ember days; the musical Quaestiones in musica has been attributed to him. Cosmas of Prague was his student.
b.s: The work held here is his De quadratura circuli, an early medieval mathematical treatise that candidly reports the quadrature problem as unsolved — citing Aristotle, Boethius, Adelbold, Wazo, Gerbert, and Virgil.

w: Epitome of the History of the Franks
Fragments on the History of the Franks

b.bio: Fredegarius is the conventional name given since the sixteenth century (first by Claude Fauchet in 1599) to the anonymous compiler of a seventh-century Frankish chronicle running from creation to 658. No manuscript names him. Modern research finds the compilation made of texts by different hands: a Burgundian who epitomized Gregory of Tours' six books and excerpted Jerome and Idatius, and the author of the original fourth book continuing where Gregory's history ends. The library prints him as Fredegarius Scholasticus Burgundiae.
b.s: His Chronicle is one of the few sources for the Merovingian period after Gregory of Tours stops in 591, and the works held here — the Chronicle with its epitome and fragments — carry that continuation.

b.bio: An Anglo-Saxon monk, pupil of Alcuin at York and at the court of Charlemagne, where he was known as Nathaniel and served as a deacon and later archdeacon. He succeeded Alcuin as abbot of Saint-Martin of Tours in 804, witnessed Charlemagne's will in 811, and served Louis the Pious as archchancellor from 819; he also held the abbeys of Saint-Bertin, Saint-Omer, and Cormery. Sources differ on his death date: the Catholic Encyclopedia and Coenotur give 834 at Tours, while Howlett gives 10 August 833. He took part in controversies against Agobard of Lyon.
b.s: The library holds his De nihilo et tenebris, a short epistolary treatise answering Charlemagne's question whether nothing and darkness are something — arguing that every finite name signifies something, that nothing is therefore a great something, and that God created all things from nothing.

b.bio: Fridegodus (Frithegod), a deacon probably of Frankish origin, came to Canterbury and served Archbishop Oda as teacher and scholar, instructing the young Oswald of Worcester. Eadmer records that he was thought to excel his contemporaries in secular and divine learning. When Wilfrid's relics were translated to Canterbury around 956, Oda commissioned him to render Eddius Stephanus's prose Life of St. Wilfrid into heroic verse; the result, the Breviloquium Vitae Wilfridi, is so dense with Greek vocabulary that William of Malmesbury said it needed a sibyl to interpret it. After Oda's death he likely returned to the continent.
b.s: The library holds his verse Life of St. Wilfrid, a reworking of Eddius that defends Roman liturgical instruction against Colman and the Scots and presents Benedict's rule as the perfect norm of monastic life.

b.bio: Frederick I, son of Count Berthold I of Schwarzenburg, was a canon at Bamberg and Speyer before Emperor Henry IV appointed him Archbishop of Cologne in 1100. He backed Henry V against his father, conducted the marriage of Henry V and Matilda in 1110, helped draw up the Concordat of Worms in 1122, and in 1125 elected Lothair of Saxony as king. He died on 5 October 1131 and was buried at Michaelsberg Abbey. A later 'Archbishop Frederick of Cologne' appears in Britannica in connection with the 1394 election deliberations under Rupert II; that fourteenth-century figure is a different man and is not the author of the works held here.
b.s: The library holds his letters and diplomas from PL 166: documents defending monastic rights and church unity — asserting that communion with excommunicates alienates one from the church, that the faithful remnant constitutes the true church, that correction aims at restoration to church unity, that an ancient synodal grant secures monastic tithes, that diplomas renew rather than create rights, that anathema guards ecclesiastical privileges, and that episcopal authority confirms church possessions.

b.bio: The library prints this name for an excerpt from a diploma preserved in PL 188 alongside the chronicles of Godfrey of Viterbo. The diploma belongs to Frederick I Barbarossa, Holy Roman Emperor, who died in 1190. The sources describe him chiefly through his court: he employed Godfrey of Viterbo as secretary (notarius) and diplomat and enjoyed the confidence of Sicard of Cremona. No theological work by Frederick is recorded here; the item held is an act of imperial chancery, historical rather than doctrinal.
b.s: The single item under this name is a chancery diploma of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa printed in PL 188, not a patristic or theological text.

b.bio: Wikisource records Frigobertus only as a Frank of the seventh century, with no dates, offices, or other works. The two pages printed under his name in Migne's PL 87 are an appendix of monastic material: they treat the Trinity, sacraments, true worship, and last things in passing, but their substance is disciplinary and economic. They cite 'the rule of the holy fathers,' assert that monastics hold all things in common and that the congregation elects the abbess's successor, and legislate on almsgiving and on endowed property. The mention of an abbess suggests a community of women.
b.s: The text held here is not a theological treatise but a short monastic rule or charter fragment on communal property, succession of an abbess, and sanctions for violating endowments.

b.bio: Frollandus Sylavectensis — Frolland, bishop of Senlis — appears in the Histoire littéraire de la France under the years 1053–1063 as a writing bishop of that see. The sources consulted here give no further biographical detail: no birthplace, family, or account of his episcopate. He must not be confused with the better-attested earlier bishops of Senlis who share the shelf's geography: Liudhard (Lethard), Queen Bertha's chaplain in Kent in the late sixth century, and Rieul (Regulus), the traditional first bishop of the see. The library holds one short piece under his name.
b.s: His single surviving letter to Berengar defends prayer for the dead: the prayers of the faithful avail for others' souls and the intercession of saints aids souls after death — a position taken against Berengar's circle amid eleventh-century disputes over Eucharistic and doctrinal rigorism.

b.bio: The library's 'F.J. Fronto' is Jean Fronteau, a regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris who served as chancellor of the abbey and the university; a BNF-recorded dedication to a doctor of sacred theology printed in 1661 identifies him by these titles. He is not the Roman rhetorician Marcus Cornelius Fronto (c. 100–late 160s AD), tutor of Marcus Aurelius, whom other sources describe under a similar name; that man wrote orations and letters, not the works held here. The works under this name concern Ivo of Chartres: a short life and a dedicatory letter defending Ivo against later critics.
b.s: His two pieces here are a biography and defense of Ivo of Chartres, arguing that the investiture disputants were guilty of no heresy or schism and that lay investiture could be tolerated when peace required it.

b.bio: Frotharius (Frothar/Frothaire) of Toul was educated at the monastery of Garze, was abbot of St-Evre at Toul, and became bishop of Toul in 813 (Wikipedia's infobox records consecration by Wulfar). He served Louis the Pious in dispute resolution and palace work at Gondreville, stayed loyal during the revolt of Bernard, and sat on councils judging the rebel bishops. His death is dated c. 847 by one source and 849 or 850 by another. He left a collection of letters—21 per the Cyclopedia, 32 per Molinier—assembled partly as models, several addressed to Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis.
b.s: His letters show a ninth-century bishop's dealings with the imperial court and monasteries: restoring alienated church lands, defending monks against abbots who broke the rule (monks may appeal to imperial authority against an abbot violating the rule), and resisting royal envoys over ecclesiastical rights.

b.bio: Froumund was a Benedictine monk of Tegernsee, active as a scribe, scholasticus, and poet. He took part in the monastery's refoundation and was sent to help establish the house at Feuchtwangen, where he began his writing. His collected letters and poems survive in a single manuscript and are among the earliest such collections assembled by one author around the year 1000.
b.s: The works held here — poems and letters from PL 141 — show an Ottonian monastic writer treating sin, grace, prayer for the dead, and the duties of princes, while defending himself against those urging him to accept priesthood.

b.bio: Frowin of Engelberg was a Benedictine abbot, elected in 1142 to succeed Adelhelm as second abbot of the newly founded monastery of Engelberg in Unterwalden. His early life is unrecorded; Einsiedeln and St. Blaise both claim him as a monk, with St. Blaise the first mention. He built up the abbey's possessions and privileges, made it a double monastery with a house for nuns, founded a school teaching philosophy and theology alongside the trivium and quadrivium, and assembled a large manuscript library (containing Homer, Cicero, Cato, Ovid), lost to fire in 1729.
b.s: The works held here are a treatise on free choice addressed to Adelbert, arguing that free will is the glory of rational nature, that all science and beatitude are founded in it, that it judges all things and is judged by none, and that it bears God's image as a mirror; and an exegesis of the Lord's Prayer.

b.bio: Fulk the Younger, son of Count Fulk IV of Anjou and Bertrada of Montfort, was born at Angers between 1089 and 1092. He was count of Anjou from 1109 and count of Maine from 1110 by marriage to Erembourg. In 1129 he passed Anjou to his son Geoffrey V; in 1131 he became king of Jerusalem as husband and co-ruler of Queen Melisende, ruling until his death at Acre in November 1143 (sources give 10 or 13 November). The works held under his name are not theological treatises but donation charters: records of gifts of land and revenues to churches and monasteries, framed in the language of sin, almsgiving, and eternal reward.
b.s: These charters show how a twelfth-century prince expressed piety through endowment—founding a monastery under Benedictine rule, claiming church lands immune from secular exaction, and treating alms as goods converted from temporal to eternal.

b.bio: The library holds one brief historical epistle addressed to Pope Alexander II, naming Wido, bishop of Amiens, and Gervasius as a metropolitan among its citations, and treating matters of the Church. The letter appears to cite 'Abbot Fulk', which may indicate the author styled himself an abbot of Corbie, though this cannot be confirmed from surviving records. None of The surviving records describes this man directly: they cover Paschasius Radbertus, Ratramnus, and Fulk the Venerable, archbishop of Reims (d. 900) — different persons with similar names or connections, whose careers must not be attributed here.
b.s: His surviving letter to Pope Alexander II is preserved in PL 150 and treats ecclesiastical matters, naming figures including Wido, bishop of Amiens, and Gervasius the metropolitan.

b.bio: Fulk the Venerable succeeded Hincmar as archbishop of Reims in March 883 and died on June 17, 900. Born into a powerful aristocratic family and brother of Anscar I, Margrave of Ivrea, he had been a palace cleric of Charles the Bald and abbot of Saint-Bertin by 877. He was a central figure in West Frankish politics after the fall of the Carolingian empire: he backed his kinsman Guy II of Spoleto for the throne in 888, then turned to Arnulf and finally crowned the young Charles at Reims in 893, holding that only a Carolingian could rightfully be king. Most knowledge of his career comes from Flodoard's History of the Church of Reims, which preserves summaries of some 76 letters.
b.s: The library holds two pages of his letters (PL 131), which defend Reims's primacy among Gallican churches, assert obedience to the apostolic see, rebuke King Charles the Bald and his counselors, and argue that bishops may excommunicate an erring emperor.

w: In Which the Fragments of the Diocese of Meaux Are Enumerated

b.bio: A Latin verse-writer born at Beauvais who died at Meaux in the eleventh century. The authority file for Fulcoius Bellovacensis records his death under 1084 and lists 'Foulcoie de Meaux' and 'Fulcoius Meldensis subdiaconus' among his name-forms, so the library's 'of Meaux' is one designation for the Beauvais poet. Encyclopedia.com calls him an archdeacon and a writer of Latin verse active through the later eleventh century; the Tübingen/IxTheo record styles him a subdeacon. He composed three books of verse — Uter (epitaphs and letters), Neuter (lives of saints), and Uterque (a biblical narrative on Christ and His Church) — and corresponded with ecclesiastical and political leaders.
b.s: His surviving pieces here are short historical and epistolary fragments from PL 150 — an enumeration of the diocese of Meaux, a letter to Hugh, and an epitaph — valued chiefly as evidence of eleventh-century clerical verse and reform-era correspondence.

b.bio: Sources under this name describe at least two different men: Francisco Antonio González Oña (Casar de Talamanca 1773–Madrid 1833), priest, Hebraist, professor of Arabic and Hebrew at Alcalá, senior librarian of the Biblioteca Real and secretary of the Real Academia Española; and Francisco Antonio González Laguna (1729–1799), a Spanish-born Franciscan friar and botanist in Lima. Neither source confirms which, if either, wrote the prefatory material printed in PL 84, so no dates or offices are asserted for the author of the text held here.
b.s: The seven pages held here are a prefatory essay on the ancient Spanish canonical collection (the Hispana), arguing that Spain possessed its own canon law corpus distinct from Dionysius's, compiled at the Fourth Council of Toledo, that the pseudo-Isidore ('Isidore Mercator') collection is not Spanish but forged and corrupted Spanish canons in Gaul, and defending Martin of Braga's compilation against claims for Isidore of Setabis — positions set against Justel, Cajetanus Cenni, and Joseph Saenz de Aguirre.

w: Essay on the Foundation of the School of Saint-Victor

b.bio: The sources describe several men named Flavian — a fifth-century Archbishop of Constantinople and a sixth-century Patriarch of Antioch — none of whom wrote these works. The record's items are nineteenth-century historical studies printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 175, PL 196), which match Flavien-Abel-Antoinin Hugonin, born at Thodure on 4 July 1823, ordained priest of Paris in 1850, confirmed Bishop of Bayeux (-Lisieux) in 1867 until his death on 2 May 1898, and a Council Father at Vatican I. His pieces here treat the origins of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, arguing that William of Champeaux founded its school, that the chapel preceded the abbey, and correcting Lobineau, Hélyot, Sauval, and Du Boulay; another notices Richard of Saint-Victor.
b.s: His works here are foundational studies on the school and abbey of Saint-Victor and on Richard of Saint-Victor, prefixed to the relevant PL volumes.

b.bio: Friedrich Lindenbrog (Latinized Tiliobroga), born in Hamburg on 28 December 1573, son of the notary Erpold Lindenbrog, studied at Helmstedt (enrolled 1592) and then at Leiden under Justus Lipsius and Joseph Justus Scaliger, who introduced him to Paris scholarly circles. After travels in England, France, and Italy he took the licentiate of laws at Basel in 1608 and practiced as an advocate in Hamburg, where the Senate sent him to London in 1614 to settle disputes over the contracts of the resident English merchants. He died in Hamburg on 9 September 1648. The works printed here under his name are his editions of Merovingian formulae — legal formularies citing Marculf and other ancient collections — not patristic texts.
b.s: A reader holding these pages has not a church father but the early modern jurist-philologist whose editions of Frankish legal formulae preserved documents on episcopal appointment, ecclesiastical immunity from public judges, and irrevocable royal grants.

b.bio: Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana y Butrón was born at León on 22 September 1722 and died at Rome on 17 April 1804. After studies at the Jesuit college of his native city he took a canonry in Toledo, became Bishop of Plasencia in 1765, Archbishop of Mexico from 1766 to 1771, then Archbishop of Toledo from 1771 to 1800. Pius VI made him cardinal in 1789; he served as Grand Inquisitor of Spain from 1794 to 1797. He published the acts of the first three provincial councils of Mexico (1769–70) and edited historical and liturgical documents, including the works of Isidore of Seville and materials on the Hispanic (Mozarabic) rite.
b.s: The pieces held here are his editorial apparatus — prefaces, admonitions to the reader, and extracts — for Migne's volumes of Isidore, Ildephonsus, Gregory, and related texts, in which he defends the apostolic origin and antiquity of the Mozarabic rite against those who would reduce all worship to a single Roman use.

b.bio: The library holds a single item under this name: an index of homilies and sermons printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 165. No source consulted identifies a person called Franciscus Aelius Marchesius. Two distinct medieval figures with similar names appear in the sources — John Marchesinus, an Italian Franciscan of the late thirteenth/early fourteenth century who wrote the Mammotrectus super Bibliam at Reggio Emilia, and Francis of Marchia (born c. 1285–1290 at Appignano del Tronto, lectured on the Sentences at Paris in 1319–20, later at Avignon), a Franciscan theologian allied with Ockham and Michael of Cesena against Pope John XXII. Neither matches this name as printed, so neither is asserted to be the author here.
b.s: The work held is an index of homilies and sermons in PL 165, useful only as a finding aid to that volume's contents.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a person named Franciscus Oliverius: the attached biographies concern Franciscus Lucas Brugensis (1548/49–1619), Franciscus Quaresmius (1583–1650), and Petrus Iohannis Olivi (d. 1298), none of whom match the name or the works held here, and they may not be used for this note. What the library record itself shows is an author represented by two short pieces in the Patrologia Latina — a one-page eulogy (PL 74) and an epistle (PL 127) — treating grace, Christ as true God and savior, and miracles worked by saints after death. Beyond that, nothing can be asserted about his life, dates, or office.
b.s: His presence in this library rests on two brief Patrologia Latina pieces: a eulogy crediting grace for recording the lives of the virtuous and attesting posthumous miracles of saints, and an epistle on Christ's divinity.

b.bio: This entry covers an anonymous collective author: the fathers of a church council whose acts are printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 105 under the heading 'Patres concilii'. No individual names, dates, or sees are attached to the record held here, which consists only of the preface to those acts. the surviving records with this note describe other persons entirely — Paterius of Brescia (d. 606), compiler of Gregory the Great's exegesis, and various named Latin Fathers — none of whom is this author.
b.s: The work held here is the preface to conciliar acts in PL 105; it appears to relate to the proceedings of a church council rather than the teaching of any single writer, though no further details are available from the library record.

b.bio: No source consulted identifies a 'Francesco Quadrato' matching this library's record. The sources describe three different men under similar names: Francesco Quattrone, a twentieth-century Calabrian cleric and Latin poet (source:1); Francesco Saverio Quadrio, a Jesuit-turned-secular literary historian of Valtellina, 1695–1756 (sources:2–3); and an early Bishop of Malta who died around 100 (source:4). None of these can be tied to the single-page dedication letter held here under this name in PL 150, so nothing about dates, offices, or biography can be asserted for the author as printed.
b.s: The work held here is only a dedication letter (PL 150); its author cannot be identified from surviving records.

w: On the Life and Writings of St. Hildegard

b.bio: The library prints this name on a two-page notice on the life and writings of Hildegard of Bingen, prefixed to her works in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 197. the surviving records describe other men named Reuss and cannot be attached to this author with confidence: one is a Redemptorist, Franciscus Xaverius Reuss, born at Bergheim in Alsace in 1842; another is Francis X. Reuss of Columbia, Pennsylvania (born 1847), a Catholic historian and newspaperman who wrote parish chronicles and a biographical cyclopaedia of the American hierarchy. Neither source mentions the Hildegard notice, so no dates or offices are asserted here.
b.s: His two pages introduce Hildegard to Latin readers: they argue that her visions came while awake through inner senses, rank Elisabeth of Schönau as closest to her, identify Scivias as her principal visionary work, mark certain prophecies as spurious attributions, and point to Wiesbaden codices preserving unpublished material.

w: Historical and literary notice on Salvian
Historical and literary notice on St. Nicetas
Historical and literary notice on St. Patrick
Notice concerning the editions of Chrysologus

b.bio: Fredericus G. Schoenemannus is the Latinized form of Gerhard (Gerard) Schneemann, a German Jesuit born at Wesel on the Lower Rhine on 12 February 1829 and died at Kerkrade in the Netherlands on 20 November 1885. After studying law he entered the seminary at Münster, joined the Society of Jesus on 24 November 1851, and was ordained priest on 22 December 1856. He taught philosophy at Bonn and Aachen, then lectured on church history and canon law at Maria Laach. He edited the Stimmen aus Maria-Laach for six years from 1871 and was chief promoter of the Collection Lacensis (Acta et decreta sacrorum conciliorum recentiorum), dying while preparing Vatican I documents for its final volume.
b.s: The works held here are his historical and literary notices prefacing volumes of Migne's Patrologia Latina — introductions to Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose, Chrysologus, Salvian, Zeno and other Fathers — which is why this library files him under Latin Fathers.

b.bio: Fl. Valia Q. Theudovius is represented in this collection by a single item under his name: the Cornutian Charter, four pages recording the terms of an ecclesiastical endowment.
b.s: The Cornutian Charter matters as a legal text on church property: it asserts that donations must never be alienated, binds future additions to the same condition, gives heirs a right to reclaim alienated gifts, reserves lifetime usufruct of lands for the donor, notes that 'ostrea' is a scribal error for 'ostia', derives vestment names from material origin and color, and cites authorities including Hadrian I, Petrus Rotari, Sixtus III, Paschal I, Panvinius, Cangius, Damasus, and Plinius.

b.bio: Ferdinando Ughelli was a Florentine Cistercian, born 21 March 1595 into a prominent family. He entered the order in 1610 and studied at the Gregorian University in Rome under the Jesuits Francesco Piccolomini and John de Lugo. He served as prior of Cestello, abbot of San Galgano (1628–1631), abbot of Nonantola (1632), abbot of Badia a Settimo near Florence, and from 1638 abbot of Tre Fontane in Rome, where he is buried. He helped revise Ciacconius' lives of the popes and cardinals (Vatican Press, 1630), was consultor of the Index and theologian to Cardinal Carlo de' Medici, and declined offers of episcopal office.
b.s: His nine-volume Italia sacra sive de episcopis Italiæ (Rome, 1643–62) assembled the episcopal histories of every Italian diocese from the earliest Christian centuries to his own day; the notices held here are his historical accounts of individual sees and churches as printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina.

b.bio: Francesco Antonio Zaccaria was a Venetian Jesuit, born 27 March 1714, ordained priest at Rome in 1740. He taught grammar and rhetoric at Gorizia, succeeded Muratori as ducal archivist and librarian of Modena in 1751, and was removed in 1768 for his Antifebronio defending the rights of the Holy See against Febronius. He then served as librarian at the Jesuit professed house in Rome; Pius VI later made him professor of church history at the Sapienza and director of the Accademia de' Nobili Ecclesiastici. Sommervogel ascribes 161 printed works to him, chiefly on church history, episcopal series, and apologetics for the Bollandist Acta Sanctorum.
b.s: The library holds his philological annotations on PL 82, where he defends corrected readings (milliastae not miliciastae; creationis not creatoris) in patristic texts and argues against misreadings by Chacon, Grialius, and others.
